newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels dig in despite Berisha amnesty.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels dig in despite Berisha amnesty.

text.p: Armed rebels behind barricades in Albania's southern towns of Sarande and Vlore refused to lay down their weapons on Friday despite an amnesty offer to the insurgents from President Sali Berisha.

The United States and Europe welcomed Berisha's move to suspend the army's advance south to end the rebellion and urged the president, the ruling Democrats and opposition parties to reach a political settlement to end the crisis.
Rebel committees in the Adriatic towns of Sarande and Vlore, where rioting and looting broke out last weekend, said they would not surrender their arms until Berisha stepped down.

"We're not giving up our weapons until Berisha resigns," Fuat Karali, a former police officer and now a member of Sarande's rebel council told a mass rally in the town square witnessed by a Reuters reporter.
Barricades were strengthened around the Adriatic coastal town of some 15,000 people, visible from the Greek holiday island of Corfu, and people were preparing for a long siege.
The message appeared the same from the port of Vlore, 160 km (110 miles) north of Sarande.
"They said the amnesty will not satisfy them. They want President Berisha to resign and they want their money back," a Western reporter who reached the town told Reuters by telephone.

Nearly half of Vlore's 80,000 people, as well as hundreds of thousands of other people across the country of 3.4 million, had invested their savings in pyramid investment schemes which crumbled in January.

The demise of pyramid schemes at the beginning of the year sparked weeks of protests which erupted into anarchy last weekend as rioters went on the rampage, seizing arms from police and army depots and looting shops. At least 16 people have been reported killed in Vlore, many by random shooting.
Berisha, who held talks with all political parties on Thursday, called a halt to the military push and offered an amnesty if insurgents surrendered their arms by six a.m. (0500 GMT) on Sunday.
In Rome, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen welcomed the decision.
"This is primarily a political problem to be resolved and certainly not a military one, but there has been a ceasefire and that is a very productive sign," Cohen said.

In Tirana, a four-member mission of the Council of Europe called on all parties to condemn the insurgency and urged the main opposition Socialist Party to take up the seats it won in parliament last year in a disputed general election.

"All political parties should state their condemnation of acts of criminal violence and rebellion in southern Albania if these should persist despite the March 6 offer of an amnesty," the mission said in a statement.

Albania is a member of the 40-state Council of Europe, set up to promote democracy and human rights. The mission urged the government to respect the European Human Rights Convention and end restrictions on the domestic media.
